clue.text: Forgive the oath, eh? Well, some language

parts.note: to pardon someone is to forgive them
'My!' and 'Well!' are both mild exclamations of surprise
French is one language among many

explanation.surface: Someone asks forgiveness for a curse, shrugging that it is just a bit of language.
explanation.walkthrough: Unusually, the definition sits in the middle of the clue, flanked by wordplay. The whole phrase is the jokey apology said straight after swearing, so it fits 'the oath, eh?'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is a jokey apology offered immediately after uttering a swear word, so it naturally accompanies a spoken curse.

clue.text: In report, a rule virtually incomprehensible

indicators.note: virtually means almost but not quite, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a report is a loud bang, a pop

indicators.note: something incomprehensible is jumbled and makes no sense, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: the words as written, losing their last letter

explanation.surface: A regulation in some official report is almost impossible to understand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a preposition leading into the clue, but it is the definition: something in is fashionable. 'Report' means a bang, not a document.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is 'in' means it is currently fashionable and widely liked, the same as being well liked by many people.

clue.text: Mirror featuring clue so cryptic for council worker

indicators.note: a thing featuring something has it included within it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a mirror reflects light, so it is a reflector

indicators.note: cryptic means obscure or mysterious, so the letters come out disguised in a new order

parts.note: the two words as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A local newspaper column features a puzzling clue aimed at a council employee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mirror' suggests the newspaper, but it is just a reflector, split after REF to take the rearranged letters. A refuse collector is a British binman.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain, emptying household bins is a local council service, so the bin collector is a typical municipal employee.

clue.text: God of demonic invention, nefarious primarily

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so each word contributes its opening letter

parts.note: first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter

explanation.surface: A deity dreamed up by something devilish, wicked above all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primarily' seems to apply only to 'nefarious', but it covers all four words after 'God'.
explanation.definitionFit: Odin is the chief of the Norse pantheon, ruler of Asgard and father of Thor.

clue.text: Mutter when pair of drinks tipped up

indicators.note: in a down clue, tipping something up turns it upside down, so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: two glasses of rum

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles as two drinks get knocked over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tipped up' sounds like spilling drinks, but in a down clue it turns the letters upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs describe speaking quietly and indistinctly, often in low complaint, so they are close synonyms.

clue.text: Burgers, say, staff cooked: fine without starter

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters are worked into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: a starter is the first course, so lacking it means the opening letter goes

parts.note: fine means good, which then loses its first letter

explanation.surface: Kitchen staff have cooked some burgers, and they are fine, though there was no starter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' must become its synonym before losing its head; 'starter' plays on the restaurant meal of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Burgers are a classic example of quickly prepared takeaway meals; 'say' signals the definition is by example.

clue.text: Fresh loaf exited shed

indicators.note: fresh means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A just-baked loaf has left the garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed' looks like the noun for a garden hut, but it is the past tense verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To exfoliate is to cast off thin layers such as skin cells or bark, so exfoliated means having cast them off.

clue.text: Complicated contraption for capturing boron, measurer of chemical's use

indicators.note: to capture something is to hold it, so one piece is held inside the other
something complicated is tangled up, so the letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: the two words as written, to be rearranged
B is the chemical symbol for boron

explanation.surface: An elaborate lab device traps boron and measures how a chemical is used.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters of the first two words take in boron's symbol after CAR. The chemical in the definition is carbon.
explanation.definitionFit: A carbon footprint quantifies the carbon dioxide emissions caused by a person or activity, gauging how much carbon is produced.

clue.text: Put in bins tallish bags

indicators.note: to bag something is to hold it inside, so the letters are held within the words

parts.note: concealed across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone stuffs rather tall bags into the bins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bags' looks like the noun, the rubbish bags, but it is a verb meaning holds. INSTAL is the British single-L spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: To install equipment is to place and fit it in position, so 'put in' is a plain synonym.

clue.text: More inflated ego in smoker?

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

parts.note: a smoker puffs on a cigarette
the ego is the self, I

explanation.surface: Is a smoker's ego more swollen than most?
explanation.walkthrough: Ego is the Latin for I, a common crossword substitution.
explanation.definitionFit: Something puffier is more swollen or blown up with air, the comparative sense matching 'more inflated'.

clue.text: Slight cut on back of dress, orangey-yellow

indicators.note: something cut is shortened, so it loses its final letter
the back of a word is its end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: last letter
a slight is an insult, an affront; it loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A small snip on the back of an orangey-yellow dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' looks like an adjective meaning small, but it is a noun meaning an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Saffron is the spice from crocus stigmas and names the deep orange-yellow colour they give to food.

clue.text: Visiting Oslo, student — in need of a map?

indicators.note: someone visiting a place is inside it for a while, so the letters are found within the words

parts.note: concealed across the two words

explanation.surface: A student on a trip to Norway's capital wonders whether they need a map.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is by suggestion, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has lost their way would be glad of directions, so needing a map hints at being astray.

clue.text: Winter garment defective, locate elastic

parts.note: duff is British slang for faulty or useless

indicators.note: elastic stretches and changes shape, so the letters are pulled into a new form

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A winter coat is faulty; find the elastic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elastic' looks like something to find in the garment, but it is the signal to rearrange the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A duffel coat is a heavy woollen hooded overcoat with toggles, worn for warmth in cold weather.

clue.text: Before a hat removed, neck warmer?

indicators.note: removed can be read as re-moved, moved again, so the letters are shifted around

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Once the hat is off, something to keep the neck warm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Removed' reads as taking the hat off, but it signals that the letters are moved around.
explanation.definitionFit: A feather boa is a long fluffy scarf draped around the shoulders, so loosely it keeps that region cosy.

clue.text: Terrible noise hitting item

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a loud unpleasant din
second meaning: the strung bat used in tennis or squash

explanation.surface: An awful din made by something being struck.
explanation.walkthrough: The two meanings run together as if one describes the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a loud clamour and the strung bat players use to strike balls in tennis and squash.

clue.text: Leader in government would fail, not half useless — shocking!

indicators.note: without half of it, the word keeps only its first two of four letters
a leader is at the front, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter

indicators.note: something useless is broken or out of order, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the word loses its second half

explanation.surface: A political leader predicts failure: utterly useless, how dreadful!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' is a British slang intensifier meaning 'very', but here it simply cuts a word in two.
explanation.definitionFit: God-awful is an informal intensified way of saying extremely bad or appalling, matching the exclaimed sense of shocking.

clue.text: A paramour preserves energy with a cosmetic liquid

indicators.note: to preserve something is to keep it safe inside, so one piece is held within another

parts.note: a paramour is a lover
E is the symbol for energy in physics
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lover keeps up their energy using a beauty product.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preserves' suggests jam or keeping fit, but it means holding a letter inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Aloe vera is the gel from a succulent plant, widely used in skin creams and lotions for soothing skin.

clue.text: With due respect, Eliot busy in work

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

parts.note: to ply a trade is to work at it

indicators.note: someone busy is bustling about, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Respectfully, the poet T. S. Eliot was hard at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eliot' suggests the poet, but the name is just five letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something courteously means showing proper regard and good manners to others, the sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Animal poked by sharp object, shrill of voice

indicators.note: to be poked is to be jabbed into, so here the second piece is pushed inside the first

parts.note: a pig is a farm animal
a pin is a small sharp object

explanation.surface: A creature jabbed with something sharp squeals in a high-pitched voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Animal' could be many things; only a three-letter farm animal splits neatly around the sharp object.
explanation.definitionFit: A piping voice is thin and high-pitched, like the sound of a small pipe or whistle.

clue.text: Extra time

definitions.meaning: first meaning: additional, as in a further helping

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as football's extra time, but the two words are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means additional or another; as a noun it is the basic unit of measured duration.

clue.text: And sure to perform — is he?

definitions.text: And sure to perform — is he?

indicators.note: performing involves acting out a part, so the letters take on a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is certain to put on a show: is he that kind of performer?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: a man certain to perform is a professional dancer.
explanation.definitionFit: A danseur is a male ballet dancer, someone who performs on stage; the question hints that 'he' is one.

clue.text: Was successful at football and made an impression?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: put the ball in the net for a goal
second meaning: marked a surface with a cut or line

explanation.walkthrough: 'Made an impression' sounds like impressing people, but it is a literal mark scratched into something.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both netting a goal in a match and cutting a groove or line into a surface.

clue.text: Choice note on piano

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another follows it, so the word before this is placed after the word after it

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
a note can be a reference, as in a citation or testimonial

explanation.surface: Picking which note to play on the piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' suggests music, but it means a written reference; 'on' places it after the musical abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A preference is the option one favours or selects over others, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Turn blunted needle

indicators.note: blunting removes a sharp point, so the word loses its tip, its final letter

parts.note: a spine is a sharp needle, as on a cactus or hedgehog

explanation.surface: Twisting a needle that has lost its point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needle' suggests sewing, but here it is a spine such as a cactus or hedgehog has; blunting it takes off the end letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To spin is to rotate or revolve, the same motion as turning round.

clue.text: Yankee's successor, Southern African

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in the NATO phonetic alphabet, the word after Yankee (Y)
second meaning: a member of a people of South Africa

explanation.walkthrough: 'Yankee' suggests an American, but it is the radio code word for Y, followed by the code word for Z.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both the radio alphabet word for Z and the name of a large Bantu people of KwaZulu-Natal.

clue.text: Bigwig, unskilled?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, read as two words: lacking ability, incapable

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second meaning needs the word split in two: not able.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun it means a prominent important person; split into two words it means lacking the capacity to do something.

clue.text: Standard defeat in race, ultimately

parts.note: a rout is a crushing defeat
taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: last letter

explanation.surface: In the end, losing a race is the usual outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a linking preposition, but it is kept as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Routine describes something ordinary and done as normal practice, matching standard as an adjective.

clue.text: Ordinary study in small hotel, say

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

parts.note: B and B, a bed and breakfast, is a small guesthouse
to read a subject is to study it at university
to utter is to say

explanation.surface: An ordinary study room in a little hotel, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example' but is the verb. In Britain one 'reads' a subject at university, meaning studies it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread-and-butter describes everyday basic matters, the routine staple work, so it means commonplace.
